messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Liam is a 28-year-old social media manager who left the Army several years ago and now works in an open-plan marketing office where much of the day is spent scanning video clips, tracking trends, and coordinating campaigns. During his deployment, the moment that has stayed with him in the most broken way happened during what had seemed like an ordinary convoy movement. He was riding in a vehicle with other soldiers when an explosion struck nearby. What he remembers is not a smooth sequence but jagged fragments: the metallic force of the blast, the sensation of being trapped in the vehicle with other bodies, flashes of visible wounds on the men around him, and the chopping aircraft sound overhead as helicopters came in. Large sections are missing. At times he is hit with the same terror and helplessness without any picture attached to it, only the emotional force arriving all at once. Other times the whole thing feels so extreme and disjointed that he struggles to believe it really happened to him, as if it belongs to someone else’s life.

In the months after returning home, specific cues in ordinary life began to carry the event back into the present. Seeing visible injuries on strangers—a cyclist with blood on his shin, a coworker showing stitches after a minor procedure—could make his body surge before he had even formed a thought. The sound of helicopters over the city stopped him in place. Riding in a car with someone else driving was especially potent; being a passenger gave him the same trapped feeling he had felt in the convoy. In those moments he became intensely physically reactive, his chest tightening and muscles bracing, and if someone touched him unexpectedly he jerked hard with alarm. At night he found it difficult to fall asleep because part of him felt he had to stay alert, as though letting his guard down would be dangerous.

Because these reminders brought back either disconnected pieces of the convoy attack or raw emotion with no image, Liam began organizing his life around not setting them off. He avoided military or police uniforms and any visible weapons, crossing streets to stay clear of officers or leaving places early if a uniformed person came in. He avoided strenuous physical activity because an elevated heart rate and bodily strain felt too close to the state he remembered from the attack. He also started rehearsing conversations before almost any interaction, wanting to control every exchange and avoid being caught off guard. The more he lived this way, the less his memory ever settled into something coherent; it stayed in fragments and surges rather than becoming a story he could place in the past.

His work has become one of the places where the pattern is most visible. As a social media manager, he cannot fully avoid images from the public world, and when injury footage appears unexpectedly on a feed he feels a jolt of recognition before he can scroll away. On days when news clips include aircraft audio or emergency scenes, he becomes guarded for hours, speaks only after silently scripting what he plans to say, and avoids riding with coworkers to lunch or client meetings. If someone claps him on the shoulder from behind, he reacts sharply enough that colleagues notice. Those incidents leave him feeling exposed and different, and he has come to believe that he is permanently changed for the worse. He compares himself harshly to other people, thinking someone else would not have ended up so shaken or so unable to handle simple things like car rides or casual contact.

Over time, those beliefs have made the world feel even narrower. Because he sees himself as damaged and fundamentally outside ordinary civilian life, uniforms, weapons, injuries, and even the sound of aircraft seem to stand out more quickly to him, as if his mind is always finding proof that he does not belong anywhere fully safe. The more vigilant he becomes—especially at night and in situations where he cannot control what happens—the more he relies on avoidance to get through the day, and the more his body reacts when reminders break through anyway. Avoiding rides with others, steering clear of physically stressful situations, and overpreparing every conversation have begun to strain his relationship; his partner experiences him as distant and tense, particularly when he refuses spontaneous plans or flinches from unexpected touch.

Liam sought help after a recent week in which several things collided: helicopter sounds over his neighborhood, an injured pedestrian outside his office, and a mandatory work trip that would have required sharing a car with coworkers. He found himself unable to sleep, increasingly on edge, and ashamed by how much effort it took just to appear normal at work. What frightens him most is the sense that this is who he is now—cut off from other people, permanently altered, always one reminder away from feeling trapped again. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that the memories might stop arriving as disconnected force and that he might someday sit in a car beside someone he trusts without feeling his whole body prepare for catastrophe.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows triggers causing memories, threat, and avoidance, but it does not state in the same paragraph that reminders directly lead Liam to negative beliefs about himself or the world.

The vignette describes negative beliefs making cues like uniforms, weapons, injuries, and aircraft stand out more, but it does not clearly state within a paragraph that negative appraisals themselves generate or intensify triggers as reminders.
The vignette links reminders to fragmented memory and to physiological alarm, but it does not explicitly convey that the trauma memory itself leads to a sense of current threat in the same paragraph.

Although the memory is described as fragmented and emotionally forceful, the vignette does not explicitly state in one paragraph that the memory leads Liam to negative appraisals about himself or his situation.
The vignette does not explicitly state within a paragraph that Liam’s trauma memory causes him to notice, seek out, or become more sensitive to triggers/reminders.
The vignette describes threat leading to vigilance and avoidance, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that feeling threatened makes reminders/triggers stand out or recur.

The vignette describes avoidance maintaining fragmented memory and negative beliefs appearing elsewhere, but it does not explicitly connect maladaptive strategies as causing or worsening negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
The vignette shows vigilance and avoidance co-occurring, but it does not explicitly state within a paragraph that maladaptive strategies themselves increase Liam’s sense of threat.
